---
title: "MedSAM and SAM-Med2D: Adapting SAM for Medical Images"
---

MedSAM and SAM-Med2D are two of the most referenced SAM adaptation papers in medical imaging AI. They represent two different design philosophies for the same problem.

## Why SAM struggles on medical images

SAM was trained on SA-1B: 11 million natural images containing people, animals, objects, and scenes. When you point it at a chest CT or a pathology slide, it faces a substantial domain shift.

```text
Natural images                 Medical images
--------------                 --------------
- RGB, well-lit                - Grayscale CT/MR/X-ray, HU windowing
- Clear edges                  - Fuzzy boundaries, such as tumors or edema
- Whole, isolated objects      - Overlapping anatomy, partial volume
- Few classes per scene        - Tiny lesions inside large organs
- "What is this?" is obvious   - Requires expert prior knowledge
```

The image encoder produces features tuned for distinctions like dog versus couch versus floor, not ground-glass opacity versus consolidation. This is a classic domain shift problem, and the two papers solve it differently.

## MedSAM

Ma et al., Nature Communications 2024.

Philosophy: do not change the architecture much. Feed it enormous amounts of medical data and use the most reliable prompt type.

### Dataset

MedSAM was trained on a curated dataset of about 1.57 million medical image-mask pairs, spanning roughly 10 imaging modalities and over 30 cancer types.

Modalities include CT, MRI, X-ray, ultrasound, dermoscopy, endoscopy, fundus photography, mammography, OCT, and pathology.

### Architectural changes

The architectural changes are minimal:

```text
+-----------------+       +-----------------+       +--------------+
| Image Encoder   | ----> | Prompt Encoder  | ----> | Mask Decoder |
| ViT-B           |       | BOX ONLY        |       |              |
| fine-tuned      |       | frozen          |       | fine-tuned   |
+-----------------+       +-----------------+       +--------------+
      FULL                    FROZEN                    FULL
  fine-tuning                                      fine-tuning
```

Two key decisions matter.

First, MedSAM uses bounding-box prompts only. It deliberately drops point and mask prompts. The reason is clinical: bounding boxes provide an unambiguous spatial specification of the target, avoiding the ambiguity that points can introduce in medical images.

A point on a lung nodule could mean the nodule, the surrounding ground-glass opacity, or the whole lobe. A box leaves less room for ambiguity.

Second, the prompt encoder is frozen. Since the box format is unchanged, there is little reason to retrain it.

The model is fine-tuned end-to-end on the medical dataset: the image encoder and mask decoder weights are both updated.

### Strengths and limits

- Simple, reliable, and well validated across modalities.
- Box-only prompting fits many radiology workflows, because drawing a box around a lesion is natural.
- No point/click interaction, so it is less flexible than fully interactive SAM.
- It does not bridge the 2D to 3D gap; CT and MR are still handled slice by slice.

## SAM-Med2D

Cheng et al., 2023, OpenGVLab.

Philosophy: be comprehensive: bigger data, all prompt types, and parameter-efficient adapters so the huge encoder can be fine-tuned cheaply.

### Dataset

SAM-Med2D was built on approximately 4.6 million images and 19.7 million masks collected from public and private datasets.

That is roughly three times MedSAM's image count, with a much larger mask count because medical images often contain multiple annotated structures per image.

### Architectural changes

SAM-Med2D fine-tunes all three SAM components, but uses a clever trick on the image encoder.

```text
+----------------------------------+     +------------------+     +--------------+
| Image Encoder (ViT)              | --> | Prompt Encoder   | --> | Mask Decoder |
|                                  |     | point + box +    |     |              |
| ViT weights mostly FROZEN        |     | mask             |     | fine-tuned   |
| Adapter layers TRAINED           |     | fine-tuned       |     | full         |
+----------------------------------+     +------------------+     +--------------+
```

The big architectural innovation is adapter layers.

### What is an adapter?

An adapter is a small bottleneck neural network inserted inside every transformer block of the frozen ViT. The original SAM weights are kept frozen. Only the small adapters are trained.

Inside one transformer block of the image encoder:

```text
+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| input --> frozen Self-Attention --> frozen MLP --> output    |
|              |                         |                     |
|              v                         v                     |
|            Adapter                   Adapter                 |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+
```

Each adapter has a bottleneck structure:

```text
input
  |
  v
+-----------------+
| Down-projection |   e.g. 768 -> 64 dims
+-----------------+
  |
  v
ReLU activation
  |
  v
+---------------+
| Up-projection |   e.g. 64 -> 768 dims
+---------------+
  |
  v
+ residual connection
  |
  v
output
```

The adapter learns a small correction to the frozen feature, nudging it from natural image space toward medical image space.

### Why adapters matter

```text
Approach                 Trainable parameters   GPU memory   Main risk
--------                 --------------------   ----------   ---------
Full fine-tuning ViT-H   about 636M             huge         catastrophic forgetting
Adapter only             few million, ~1-5%     small        much safer
```

This is part of a broader family called parameter-efficient fine-tuning, or PEFT: adapters, LoRA, and prefix tuning. The term is worth knowing because it appears everywhere in modern model adaptation.

### Comprehensive prompt support

Unlike MedSAM, SAM-Med2D fine-tunes the prompt encoder using point, bounding-box, and mask information, while updating the mask decoder through interactive training.

Interactive training means the model is trained to handle iterative click refinement: click once, see a mask, click a correction, then see a better mask. This mimics how a radiologist would actually use an interactive segmentation tool.

## Side-by-side comparison

```text
                         MedSAM                    SAM-Med2D
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
Data size                ~1.57 M pairs             ~4.6 M images,
                                                   ~19.7 M masks

Image encoder            Full fine-tune            Frozen + adapters
                         changes all weights       PEFT, ~few % params

Prompt encoder           Frozen                    Fine-tuned
                         box only                  point + box + mask

Mask decoder             Fine-tuned                Fine-tuned

Interactivity            Box-only, one-shot        Click refinement
supported

Best for                 Lesion-in-box             Interactive
                         workflows                 annotation tools

Philosophy               Minimal change,           Comprehensive change,
                         mass data                 parameter-efficient
```

## What I would tell a radiologist starting out

For work in a Radiology AI Unit, the practical takeaways are straightforward.

If you have a click-to-annotate UI in mind, such as helping a resident speed up segmentation by clicking on a lesion, SAM-Med2D is the more natural fit because it handles points and iterative refinement.

If your workflow is draw a box, get a mask, such as for tumor measurement or RECIST-style use, MedSAM is robust and easier to deploy.

Both are 2D models. For volumetric CT/MR, there are several options:

- Apply the model slice by slice. This is the simplest approach and what many clinical tools do.
- Use MedSAM2, which adds memory across slices for video and 3D-style workflows.
- Use 3DSAM-Adapter or MA-SAM, which insert 3D adapters.

The adapter pattern from SAM-Med2D is the mental model to keep. Almost every modern medical foundation model adaptation, whether for segmentation, classification, or detection, uses some variant of PEFT such as adapters or LoRA.

Understanding why we freeze the big backbone and train small modules is one of the most useful concepts in this field today.

Both MedSAM and SAM-Med2D are available through Hugging Face or GitHub with PyTorch checkpoints, so they can be tried directly in a Jupyter notebook.

## Suggested next steps

- MedSAM2 and SAM 2: how memory and 3D context get added to SAM for video and volumetric data.
